proposals.name: Concrete Idiom Literalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar idiom is made newly apt by a specific visible element and both readings remain active; score 0 when the idiom is generic or unrelated to the drawing.
proposals.rationale: R03 makes “bring a lot to the table” literal, while R08 makes “get your act together” fit the circus parade. R14 and R56 show the same visual anchoring.

proposals.name: Exact Phonetic Pun
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a precise sound-based or spelling-based pun identifies a depicted object or role and creates a clear comic reinterpretation; score 0 when wordplay is absent, vague, or detachable from the image.
proposals.rationale: R02 fuses wreckage with Rachmaninoff, R09 turns crossword investigation into “vowel play,” and R33 makes “ewe” specifically sheep-related.

proposals.name: Polysemous Double Reading
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the same phrase supports two distinct, immediately available interpretations—one tied to the scene and one from another domain; score 0 when it has only one relevant meaning.
proposals.rationale: R07 exploits the meat’s possible sexual reading, while R45 combines mosquito behavior with a human consent discussion. R52 similarly gives “pooped” both bodily and work-related meanings.

proposals.name: Implied Causal Backstory
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption invents a concise off-panel event or history that explains why the depicted situation exists; score 0 when it merely labels, acknowledges, or ignores the visible anomaly.
proposals.rationale: R10 implies disastrous prior kitchen incidents, R35 explains the enormous dinner through an unseen attack, and R55 supplies a backstory involving a transformed sister.

proposals.name: Socially Plausible Impossible Character
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an impossible participant is given a specific social role, motive, or etiquette that makes the absurd interaction feel internally natural; score 0 when the caption only notes that the participant is unusual.
proposals.rationale: R06 treats the Grim Reaper as a coworker, while R17 and R59 give the giant mosquito party etiquette and social standing. These captions build interaction around the impossibility.

proposals.name: Escalated Stakes from Physical Danger
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption converts a visible hazard or threat into a sharper consequence, risk, or ominous premise; score 0 when it fails to engage the danger or merely describes it.
proposals.rationale: R03 turns reckless juggling into a social boast, R16 reframes Earth as a destructible object, and R60 makes the Grim Reaper the cause of an accident streak ending.

proposals.name: Deadpan Register Contrast
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when calm, ordinary, or bureaucratic language is applied to an extreme visual event and the tonal mismatch creates the joke; score 0 when the tone simply matches the scene or states the absurdity plainly.
proposals.rationale: R06 uses routine workplace language around Death, R60 uses an accident-statistic formula, and R04 treats a booby-trapped kitchen as a routine takeout decision.

proposals.name: Salient Detail Targeting
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption makes the drawing’s most distinctive concrete detail necessary to the joke; score 0 when it could accompany almost any cartoon or focuses on an incidental feature.
proposals.rationale: R14 depends on the metal detectors, R39 depends on the piano’s keys and the house’s locks, and R03 depends on the literal table and dangerous performance.

proposals.name: Multi-Element Integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when two or more separate visual details interact to produce one unified comic meaning; score 0 when the caption uses only one broad premise or lists details without connecting them.
proposals.rationale: R16 links the Earth piñata, the angels’ boss, and the six-day creation story. R39 links the piano’s 88 keys with the damaged house’s missing locks, while R03 combines the table and performance hazards.

proposals.name: Structural Cultural Reframing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable outside domain supplies a structural analogy for the scene, not merely a topical reference; score 0 when the reference is a name-drop with no meaningful mapping.
proposals.rationale: R24 and R34 map circus performers onto political slates and tickets. R25 similarly maps the wolf’s disguise shop onto a White House collection.

proposals.name: Compactness With a Landing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption delivers complete comic meaning in very few words, with its final word or phrase providing the landing; score 0 when it is padded, explanatory, or lacks a decisive ending.
proposals.rationale: R02, R33, and R39 achieve their turns in extremely compressed language. Their final word or phrase carries the image-specific reinterpretation.

proposals.name: Non-Generic Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption chooses a surprising, narrowly constrained angle that could not be replaced by a generic reaction; score 0 when it offers only a routine observation or response to the anomaly.
proposals.rationale: R04’s takeout suggestion and R44’s remote comment are broadly applicable reactions. By contrast, R14’s irony reference and R39’s locks-and-keys construction are distinctive to their drawings.

proposals.name: Self-Contained Cultural Accessibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke remains understandable from the caption and drawing without obscure personal knowledge or an unexplained proper name; score 0 when its humor depends primarily on opaque outside information.
proposals.rationale: R37 depends on identifying Irving Goldstein and an old-cowhand reference, while R50 depends on an unexplained Rabbi Friedman. Their premises are less self-contained than R23’s familiar Saturn reference.

proposals.name: Conversational Speech-Act Fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording sounds like a natural utterance from someone situated in the depicted interaction and responds to the exact moment; score 0 when it reads like a detached slogan, label, or headline.
proposals.rationale: R04 sounds like a practical reply between people facing the trapped kitchen, R44 sounds like an intimate correction, and R51 uses a recognizable conversational pivot.

proposals.name: Misdirection and Reversal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording establishes an expected interpretation and then sharply changes it in the closing phrase; score 0 when there is no turn, surprise, or reinterpretation.
proposals.rationale: R31 initially sounds like a personal-space complaint before its repeated “six feet” reframes the situation. R60 begins as a safety statistic and reverses it into blaming the Grim Reaper.

proposals.name: News-cycle topicality
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the caption invokes identifiable contemporary political, public-event, or news-cycle language; do not judge whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: Live political framing can attract text-model attention independently of cartoon-specific merit. Examples include the Republican references in R05, R32, and R36, and the voting reference in R09.

proposals.name: Practiced caption discipline
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the line shows format-trained compression, economical syntax, and reliance on the cartoon without explanation; do not judge whether that discipline is good.
proposals.rationale: A serial entrant may routinely produce compact, image-dependent one-liners, leaving a practice fingerprint that can be mistaken for merit. R01 and R06 are highly compressed, as are R18 and R45.

proposals.name: Catalog typography fingerprint
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text exhibits standardized transcription habits such as lowercase openings, omitted terminal punctuation, or normalized apostrophes and dashes; do not judge whether the typography is good.
proposals.rationale: Compilation conventions can make entries resemble one another regardless of their cartoon-specific content. Lowercase, punctuation-light forms appear in R01 and R05, while dash and apostrophe handling is visible in R38 and R50.

proposals.name: Consensus pun footprint
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the caption uses the single most immediate pun or stock phrase invited by the depicted object, rather than a less expected association; do not judge whether the pun is good.
proposals.rationale: A first-thought reading may be shared by many entrants and leave a recognizable textual trace unrelated to distinctiveness. The quarter readings in R01 and R57, and the wool pun in R31, illustrate this footprint.

proposals.name: Era-coded idiom
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the caption contains dated idioms, songs, catchphrases, occupations, or slang that locate it in a particular contest era; do not judge whether the reference is good.
proposals.rationale: Long-running contests accumulate era-specific conventions and references that can bias text-only interpretation. R07 invokes an older song phrase, R19 uses old-cowhand language, and R51 uses a Sherlock Holmes formula.

proposals.name: Cultural-name familiarity load
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much understanding the caption depends on a named person, brand, institution, title, or other proper cultural reference; do not judge whether the allusion is good.
proposals.rationale: Audience familiarity with external names can influence reception independently of the line's fit to the drawing. Examples include Gibson in R25, Rachmaninoff in R45, and the White House in R52.

proposals.name: Norm-challenging register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the caption uses sexual, consent-related, bodily, violent, or otherwise socially provocative language; do not judge whether the language is good or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Provocative wording can draw attention or trigger audience reactions unrelated to cartoon-specific merit. The sexual reference in R30 and consent language in R40 are clear examples; bodily harm also appears in R54.

proposals.name: Colloquial voice markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the caption uses contractions, slang, clipped fragments, eye-dialect, or direct conversational address; do not judge whether the voice is good.
proposals.rationale: Spoken-language texture can act as a style marker for text models without indicating cartoon-specific merit. Eye-dialect appears in R07, clipped slang in R59, and conversational phrasing in R50.

proposals.name: Generic caption closure
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the line has a generic, self-contained setup-to-punch structure with an obvious semantic mapping that a general-purpose writer could readily produce; do not judge whether the joke is good.
proposals.rationale: Well-formed, immediately legible caption shapes are easy for a generic prior to nominate even when editorial taste differs. R22, R37, and R56 all use straightforward premise-to-punch constructions.

proposals.name: Copyedited syntactic symmetry
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the caption shows signs of deliberate editing or assistance through balanced clauses, parallel contrasts, exact idiom completion, or carefully controlled rhythm; do not judge whether the polish is good.
proposals.rationale: Copyediting or collaboration can leave polish that a model mistakes for cartoon-specific merit, while sometimes also improving the underlying line. Balanced constructions appear in R20 and R41, with similarly controlled phrasing in R50.

proposals.name: Central-anomaly targeting
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption hinges on the cartoon’s most visually peculiar feature; score 0 when it could fit almost any scene.
proposals.rationale: The kitchen’s extreme security drives R07, and the living-room circus drives R19; both demonstrate value from targeting the central visual anomaly.

proposals.name: Multi-detail integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one joke meaningfully connects several concrete visual details; score 0 when it uses only a broad premise or one incidental object.
proposals.rationale: R26 combines the table, unicycle, and juggling hazards, while R57 combines piano keys, house, and locks into one construction.

proposals.name: In-world causal explanation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption supplies a coherent reason for the absurd situation; score 0 when it is unrelated or contradicts the depicted world.
proposals.rationale: R08 explains the enormous meat through an imagined consequence, and R49 turns the kitchen traps into a coherent family backstory.

proposals.name: Character-voiced perspective
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line clearly sounds like something the depicted character would say or think; score 0 when no speaker or viewpoint is plausibly established.
proposals.rationale: The bear’s firsthand perspective is strong in R21 and R55, where the caption naturally explains its unusual shopping behavior.

proposals.name: Role-reversal insight
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption exploits an unexpected reversal between human, animal, or social roles; score 0 when it merely restates that the scene is unusual.
proposals.rationale: R02 uses the wolf’s predatory identity within a clothing-store scenario, while R17 reverses the expected shepherding relationship into theatrical directing.

proposals.name: Cultural-frame mapping
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption maps the whole image onto a recognizable cultural, political, or social frame with clear visual correspondences; score 0 when it is an arbitrary name-drop.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R23 reinterpret the circus ensemble as political candidate groupings, while R52 applies vote-searching to indoor metal detectors.

proposals.name: Surprise reinterpretation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the ending forces a sharp, understandable second reading of the setup; score 0 when the punchline is predictable description without a turn.
proposals.rationale: R41 pivots from an ordinary restaurant shutdown to a historical threat, and R54 transforms a family scene into the aftermath of a magical wish.

proposals.name: Comic escalation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption heightens the cartoon’s absurdity into a fitting comic consequence; score 0 when it leaves the premise flat or changes the subject.
proposals.rationale: R03 escalates oversized grilling into a suggestive family spectacle, while R35 extends the creature-like tunnel into an impending bodily consequence.

proposals.name: Conversational timing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording feels like an immediate, naturally timed reaction to the pictured moment; score 0 when it sounds stilted, explanatory, or detached.
proposals.rationale: The clipped reaction in R06 and the domestic accusation in R32 both gain force from sounding like spontaneous dialogue within the scene.

proposals.name: Concise completeness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a compact line is grammatically complete, self-contained, and delivers its setup and payoff; score 0 when it is bloated, fragmentary, or requires missing context.
proposals.rationale: R01 achieves a complete premise and pun in five words, and R20 compresses the piano-house situation into a self-contained line.

proposals.name: Local pun craftsmanship
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a precise sound, spelling, or word substitution is immediately triggered by the image and remains intelligible; score 0 when the wordplay is forced or opaque.
proposals.rationale: R31’s sheep pun, R39’s musical-name distortion, and R50’s crossword wording show image-triggered lexical mechanisms with different degrees of precision.

proposals.name: Controlled boundary-pushing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an edgy, dark, or suggestive implication is clearly anchored to the cartoon and used for a purposeful punchline; score 0 when shock value is gratuitous, confusing, or offensive without comic structure.
proposals.rationale: R03 uses sexual ambiguity within the oversized-meat scene, while R45 turns consent language toward the mosquito’s exposed-skin behavior.

proposals.name: Offscreen narrative continuity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption implies a specific before-and-after story that naturally extends the pictured moment; score 0 when it offers no temporal or narrative context beyond the visible scene.
proposals.rationale: R13 invents a prior accident-free record ending with the Reaper’s arrival, and R56 implies a history of managing an unexpectedly large flock.

proposals.name: Familiar-phrase transformation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable idiom, lyric, title, or saying is altered so its new wording precisely fits the image; score 0 when the phrase is used unchanged or the reference is arbitrary.
proposals.rationale: R18 transforms the phrase about a cross word to fit a crossword, while R47 adapts pulling wool over someone’s eyes to the wolf’s disguise.

proposals.name: Non-template originality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption offers an uncommon but immediately understandable angle on the cartoon; score 0 when it relies on a stock joke pattern with little individual perspective.
proposals.rationale: R21’s detailed bear-versus-river comparison and R52’s political interpretation of metal detectors demonstrate distinctive angles beyond generic object labeling.

proposals.name: Live-news topicality
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain explicit current-affairs markers whose meaning depends on a particular week, such as political offices, campaigns, controversies, or recent events? Score only the visible markers; do not judge caption quality or cartoon fit.
proposals.rationale: The unseen news cycle can alter familiarity with a phrase without changing the caption's intrinsic fit. Textual fingerprints include political or public-affairs references, as in R07 “republican slate of candidates” and R18 “white house collection.”

proposals.name: Format-native compression
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use a compressed, standalone one-liner that omits setup and relies on the reader to supply the visual context? Score only this structural feature; do not judge whether the compression is good or apt.
proposals.rationale: A serial entrant's practiced economy may leave terse, context-dependent lines, while practice may also sometimes improve actual writing. R01 and R33 are highly compressed, visually dependent one-liners.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the caption format

proposals.name: Explanatory backstory
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption provide causal backstory, character history, or a multi-clause explanation of why the depicted situation exists? Score only the amount of explanatory narrative; do not judge its humor or quality.
proposals.rationale: One-off drafting or assistance may produce captions that explain the premise rather than trust the image; the same drafting skill can also affect genuine writing quality. R09 supplies a family backstory, while R15 explains a bear's fishing experience at length.
proposals.upstream_parent: entrant's submission practice and editing process

proposals.name: Transcription typography
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption display compilation or transcription conventions such as lowercase styling, omitted terminal punctuation, unusual dashes, ellipses, or nonstandard apostrophes? Score only the visible typography; do not judge whether it is polished or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: The compiler's formatting choices can create a text signal unrelated to cartoon-specific merit. R01 and R03 use lowercase without terminal punctuation, while R60 contains a distinctive double-hyphen construction.

proposals.name: Insider-context specificity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption rely on unexplained proper names, private relationships, or assumed local knowledge that is not established in the caption itself? Score only the amount of assumed context; do not judge whether the reference improves the joke.
proposals.rationale: An entrant writing for a known audience may use names or private-seeming context that affect reader priors without changing cartoon fit. R22 names “rabbi friedman,” and R51 invokes “irving goldstein from brooklyn” without explanation.

proposals.name: Era-coded idiom
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain wording, slang, cultural references, or speech habits that strongly signal a particular generation or historical period? Score only the apparent era signal; do not judge whether the datedness is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: The contest era can leave traces through dated idioms and cultural allusions, which may affect text-only priors independently of cartoon-specific merit. R44 uses “my dear watson,” while R51 and R58 use retro-coded phrases such as “old cowhand” and “comin' round the mountain.”
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the long-running contest series

proposals.name: Consensus-angle obviousness
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use the most salient depicted object together with its most conventional pun, idiom, or association? Score only the apparent obviousness of the angle from the cartoon description; do not judge whether the angle is funny or apt.
proposals.rationale: An entry near the consensus first-thought region may visibly name the central object and use its easiest association, regardless of intrinsic merit. R32 uses “quarter” for the coin-operated ride, R33 uses “ewe” for sheep, and R43 uses “grand” for the piano.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream for that cartoon

proposals.name: Generic caption-shaped polish
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption resemble a generally guessable good-caption template: grammatical, self-contained, instantly legible, and organized as a familiar setup-punchline or clean pun? Score only this generic form; do not judge whether an editor would prefer it.
proposals.rationale: A broadly competent writing prior can generate clean, recognizable jokes that attract generic approval, while the same competence may sometimes support genuine quality. R17, R53, and R57 use highly familiar, self-contained caption structures.

proposals.name: Taboo-register intensity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption invoke sexual material, bodily loss, death, violence, or other socially transgressive subject matter? Score only the intensity of the taboo register; do not judge whether the edge is effective or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: House norms and audience expectations can make edgy language salient independently of cartoon-specific merit. R11 invokes sexual anatomy, R23 frames exposed skin as consent, and R27 combines weight loss with amputation.
proposals.upstream_parent: magazine house style and audience tolerance

proposals.name: Stock relationship framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use familiar domestic or social roles—such as spouse, parent, child, boss, customer, or pet owner—as its main speaking frame? Score only the presence of this relational template; do not judge whether the role choice improves the caption.
proposals.rationale: A practiced entrant may repeatedly use broadly relatable relationship frames; that habit can also sometimes help actual writing. R09 uses a mother, sister, and child setup, R45 invokes “dad,” and R54 speaks from the viewpoint of a bear-parent addressing its cubs.
proposals.upstream_parent: entrant's preferred speaker and relatability template

proposals.name: Distinctive visual anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption depends on several unique objects, actions, or relationships in this cartoon; score 0 when it could fit almost any cartoon.
proposals.rationale: R09 and R44 use specific piano and house details, while R20 and R21 could apply to many domestic scenes.

proposals.name: Literal-figurative double duty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording works simultaneously as a literal description of the image and as a coherent idiom or figurative statement; score 0 when it has only one reading.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R41 make the coin-operated ride and historical pose support two meanings of “quarter,” while R28 has little such layering.

proposals.name: Exact pun construction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a sound, spelling, name, or word substitution is precise, recognizable, and tightly image-linked; score 0 when the pun is forced, vague, or absent.
proposals.rationale: R09, R39, and R46 demonstrate compact, exact wordplay tied to the piano, sheep, and crossword scenes.

proposals.name: Multiple-detail synthesis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one caption meaning coherently connects at least two distinct depicted elements; score 0 when it uses only the broad premise or an isolated object.
proposals.rationale: R17 connects the high beam, danger, and Grim Reaper, while R44 connects piano keys, house, and locks.

proposals.name: Character voice fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the implied speaker’s knowledge, attitude, and vocabulary strongly fit the depicted character; score 0 when any character could say it without adjustment.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R55 use a bear’s relationship to catching fish, while R30 supplies a comparatively interchangeable human remark.

proposals.name: Off-panel narrative
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption implies a specific prior event, relationship, or consequence that enriches the static drawing; score 0 when it adds no situation beyond what is visibly present.
proposals.rationale: R04 implies the cubs’ beliefs and the bear’s concealment, and R48 implies a transformed family member and an impending parental discovery.

proposals.name: Reinterpretive punch
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the final wording sharply reframes what the depicted action means, producing a clear second interpretation; score 0 when it merely comments on the obvious scene.
proposals.rationale: R10 reframes an indoor search through an institutional metaphor, and R31 reframes the circus intrusion through a concise public-affairs implication.

proposals.name: Deadpan tonal control
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an absurd situation is treated with calm, matter-of-fact language that heightens the humor; score 0 when the tone is excited, explanatory, or mismatched.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R17 use ordinary workplace language for impossible circumstances, preserving the visual absurdity without explaining it.

proposals.name: Non-explanatory restraint
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption adds a comic angle without simply restating the cartoon’s premise; score 0 when it only labels, summarizes, or reacts generically to what is visible.
proposals.rationale: R20, R21, and R28 mainly provide generic reactions to unusual situations, whereas R09 and R46 add independent comic mechanisms.

proposals.name: Economical completeness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when very few words establish the premise and deliver a complete punchline; score 0 when the caption is padded, incomplete, or requires substantial explanation.
proposals.rationale: R09 and R39 achieve complete jokes in extremely compact forms, while R05 spends many words describing an already visible activity.

proposals.name: Functional cultural allusion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable cultural or institutional reference directly transforms the cartoon’s specific details; score 0 when the reference is obscure, decorative, or detachable from the image.
proposals.rationale: R51 and R56 turn costume-shopping and a living-room parade into specific public-world references rather than adding unrelated name-dropping.

proposals.name: Social-world transfer
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the impossible scene becomes a sharp analogy for recognizable human behavior, norms, or institutions; score 0 when it remains a purely literal object joke with no broader implication.
proposals.rationale: R10 and R54 convert unusual physical situations into observations about social systems and interpersonal norms.

proposals.name: Edginess calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when provocative, dark, or sexual material is purposeful, proportionate, and clearly anchored to the cartoon; score 0 when it feels gratuitous, distracting, or weakly connected.
proposals.rationale: R23, R52, and R54 show how darker or more provocative angles can either derive directly from the depicted danger, bodies, or predation or become an uncontrolled distraction.

proposals.name: Spoken delivery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption has natural conversational rhythm, emphasis, and a satisfying final beat when read aloud; score 0 when it sounds awkward, overlong, or tonally flat.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R45 have clear spoken setups and landing points, while R57’s conversational exchange does not build toward a comparably shaped finish.

proposals.name: Internal-world causality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption invents a believable cause, motive, or consequence within the cartoon’s impossible world; score 0 when its statement is a non sequitur unrelated to the depicted action.
proposals.rationale: R05 gives the bear a coherent reason to buy fish, and R48 supplies a consistent magical explanation, while R57 introduces an occupation with no causal role in the scene.

proposals.name: Caption compactness
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption is highly compressed into a short phrase or minimally elaborated clause; do not judge whether this brevity is good, funny, or apt.
proposals.rationale: Length is an easy text proxy that can affect reception or model behavior without expressing cartoon-specific merit. The contrast is visible in the extremely short R02 and R14 versus the more elaborated R25 and R50.

proposals.name: List-normalization typography
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text shows raw-entry or transcription conventions such as lowercase starts, omitted terminal punctuation, doubled hyphens, repeated punctuation, or dialect apostrophes; do not judge whether the typography improves the caption.
proposals.rationale: Compilation or submission conventions leave visible formatting traces that can be predictive while being unrelated to the cartoon joke. Examples include lowercase, unpunctuated R01 and R08, and the dialect or dash usage in R24 and R30.

proposals.name: Stock setup wording
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses reusable conversational scaffolding such as ‘I think,’ ‘remember when,’ ‘I don’t know,’ ‘you should,’ or ‘let me’; do not judge whether the resulting joke is good.
proposals.rationale: A serial entrant may internalize recurring caption openings, creating a textual practice fingerprint. Such discipline may also genuinely help timing, so this is mixed; the pattern appears in R09, R23, R52, and R54.

proposals.name: Visual-premise restatement
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption explicitly repeats or paraphrases the cartoon’s visible situation or impossibility; do not judge whether the repetition is effective.
proposals.rationale: One-off or less practiced submissions may explain the image rather than assume it, leaving a detectable trace. Explanation can sometimes aid clarity, so the parent is mixed; examples include the fish premise in R03 and R25 and the resemblance premise in R11.

proposals.name: Current-affairs topicality
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption contains references to live political, public-affairs, electoral, institutional, or social-controversy language that dates it to a news moment; do not judge whether the reference fits the cartoon.
proposals.rationale: A contemporaneous news cycle can inject highly recognizable vocabulary into otherwise unrelated captions. Topicality may also genuinely improve a cartoon connection, so this is mixed; traces include R10, R15, R21, R26, and R42.

proposals.name: Era-coded idiom
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses period-marked slang, archaic wording, song or title allusions, or culturally dated phrasing; do not judge whether the wording is amusing or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: An entry’s era in the contest series can leave lexical fingerprints even when the cartoon-specific idea is unchanged. Such dating is nuisance information rather than intrinsic fit, visible in ‘two-step program’ in R17, ‘comin’ round the mountain’ in R24, and ‘old cowhand’ in R37.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the long-running contest series

proposals.name: Consensus-angle pun
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses the most immediate conventional word association invited by the drawing, such as wolf/sheep-wool, piano-keys, or ride-quarter; do not judge whether that angle is funny or publishable.
proposals.rationale: Hundreds of submissions to one cartoon can converge on its first obvious pun, creating a position-in-stream fingerprint. The association may still sometimes be genuinely apt, so this is mixed; examples include R07, R14, R20, R38, R45, and R59.

proposals.name: Role-voice anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption is framed as a direct utterance from a visually identifiable character or role, using role-specific first- or second-person perspective; do not judge whether the voice is effective.
proposals.rationale: Practiced caption writers often assign a clear speaker and maintain a compact character voice, leaving a detectable stylistic trace. Speaker choice can also genuinely improve cartoon fit, so this is mixed; examples include R02, R03, R04, and R43.

proposals.name: Magazine-safe restraint
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses a clean, non-explicit, socially restrained register, avoiding profanity, graphic sexuality or violence, and overtly abrasive language; do not judge whether restraint is desirable.
proposals.rationale: A publication’s house style can produce a stable register fingerprint independent of the particular image. That register may also contribute to actual suitability, so this is mixed; restrained examples include R04, R12, R19, and R57.
proposals.upstream_parent: house style of the contest magazine

proposals.name: Generic one-liner form
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption is a self-contained, grammatical, immediately legible conventional one-liner with a familiar setup-and-turn structure and little specialized context; do not judge whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: General-purpose writers or language models can readily nominate captions with this safe, recognizable architecture, creating a nuisance prior distinct from contest-specific merit. The form appears in R01, R07, R31, and R51.

proposals.name: Dual-Code Wordplay Activation
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if no word or phrase carries simultaneous literal-visual and figurative-idiomatic meanings. Score 10 if a key word/phrase is literally anchored in a visible element AND figuratively creates an additional comic layer, where removing either reading collapses the joke.
proposals.rationale: R22 ('you need to get your act together' — circus act + get organized) and R29 ('gravity of our situation' — physical height + seriousness) both hinge on words that are simultaneously literal to the image and figuratively idiomatic, which the dense model credits and the scorecard likely misses. R26 ('bring a lot to the table') is another prime example.

proposals.name: Unexpected Genre Reframe
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption stays within the scene's apparent genre/context. Score 10 if the caption recasts the depicted scene as belonging to an entirely different genre (political, legal, medical, commercial, etc.) that makes the visual absurdity coherently meaningful in a surprising new frame.
proposals.rationale: R01 reframes people with metal detectors indoors as a political-scene metaphor ('still looking for votes'); R30 reframes a mosquito party-crash as a legal-standards dispute ('exposed skin implies consent'). Both are dense-high/card-low because the scorecard may not reward the wholesale genre transplant.

proposals.name: Novel Linguistic Compression
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption uses only standard vocabulary and phrasing. Score 10 if the caption creates a new word, portmanteau, or uniquely compressed phrase whose humor depends entirely on this specific cartoon pairing.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('wreckmaninoff') is a one-word coinage fusing Rachmaninoff with a piano wreck; R48 ('it's so ewe') compresses a pun into three syllables. Both are dense-high/card-low, suggesting the scorecard undervalues coinage-level inventiveness.

proposals.name: Implied Off-Panel Narrative
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption merely describes or reacts to what is visibly in the cartoon. Score 10 if the caption suggests a rich backstory, timeline, or consequence extending beyond the frame that transforms understanding of the scene.
proposals.rationale: R12 implies a full magic-wish mythology (sister transformed, mommy en route, dog originally human); R36 implies a 581-day workplace safety streak shattered by the Reaper. Both are dense-high, suggesting the dense model rewards narrative depth the scorecard may not capture.

proposals.name: Satirical Target Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption references no recognizable real-world entity or only a broad generic category. Score 10 if the caption targets a precise, recognizable real-world person, institution, event, or cultural phenomenon, gaining humor from the specificity.
proposals.rationale: R10, R20, and R28 all transform a circus-parade image into specific Republican-primary satire. R46 ('white house collection') ties a wolf-in-sheep's-clothing image to a precise political referent. The dense model credits this sharpness; the scorecard may not.

proposals.name: Impact-Per-Word Efficiency
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption is long relative to its comedic payoff. Score 10 if the caption delivers a complete, layered joke in very few words (1–6 words), where every word is load-bearing and none are filler.
proposals.rationale: R08 (one word) and R20 ('he got indicted' — three words) both achieve maximal compression. R48 ('it's so ewe' — three words) similarly. The dense model rewards the efficiency; the scorecard may prefer more elaborated jokes.

proposals.name: Transcendence Over Acknowledgment
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption merely notes, explains, or comments on the visual absurdity. Score 10 if the caption adds an entirely new comic layer that makes the scene funnier than the visual alone without explaining what is weird.
proposals.rationale: R08 (doesn't explain the piano crash — adds wordplay) contrasts sharply with R44 (merely labels the cavemen as 'neanderthals'). Similarly R22 (doesn't explain the circus — adds a pun) vs. R32 (merely observes the bird is 'doing a cover'). Dense rewards transcendence; card may reward acknowledgment.

proposals.name: Dark Humor Calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption contains no dark/transgressive content, or deploys it without tonal control (merely shocking or uncomfortable). Score 10 if morbidity, transgression, or dark subject matter is deployed with precise tonal control so it reads as expertly calibrated humor.
proposals.rationale: R30 ('exposed skin implies consent') delivers darkly legalistic humor about a mosquito; R60 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') delivers deadpan horror about kitchen traps; R36 ('581 days without an accident, and then you show up') weaponizes workplace-safety language against Death. Dense rewards this; the scorecard may penalize it.

proposals.name: Caption-Image Inseparability
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption's humor would survive essentially unchanged if paired with many different cartoons. Score 10 if the caption's humor is wholly dependent on this specific image; neither caption alone nor image alone produces the joke.
proposals.rationale: R25 ('now the house has 88 keys and no locks') is meaningless without a piano-crashed house; R17 ('could you pull the wool over my eyes') only detonates against a wolf in a sheep costume. Contrast with R53 ('when I was a kid, we had to catch our own fish'), a generic 'back in my day' joke that could accompany many bear/cartoon scenarios.

proposals.name: Reader Inference Demand
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the connection between caption and image is immediately obvious or explicitly stated. Score 10 if the caption requires the reader to actively construct a non-obvious bridge between text and image, yielding satisfaction upon discovery.
proposals.rationale: R02/R04 ('no quarter will be given') requires connecting the coin-operated horse to the military idiom 'no quarter'; R43 ('i suspect vowel play') requires linking 'foul play' → 'vowel play' → crossword vowels. Dense rewards the inference gap; the scorecard may not measure it.

proposals.name: Perspective Ventriloquism
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the implied speaker or addressee is generic or ambiguous. Score 10 if humor arises from a specific, surprising speaker identity whose perspective creates a productive mismatch with the visual.
proposals.rationale: R19 ventriloquizes a bear's dismissive fishing credentials ('stood for hours in a freezing river'); R59 ventriloquizes chefs in a digestive tract with restaurant-shift banter ('we'll be pooped by the end of the night'). Dense credits the voice-specific humor; the scorecard may reward only surface cleverness.

proposals.name: Multi-Element Visual Integration
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption connects to only one visible element or to the scene generically. Score 10 if the caption simultaneously activates two or more distinct visual elements, weaving them into a single coherent joke.
proposals.rationale: R12 simultaneously activates the clothed dog on hind legs, the upset child, and an implied wish-granting backstory; R59 activates both the tunnel setting and the slow-then-busy restaurant dynamic. Dense rewards multi-element binding; the scorecard may credit single-element jokes equally.

proposals.name: Obvious-Caption Avoidance
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption is the most predictable or common type of observation for this kind of scene. Score 10 if the caption specifically avoids the obvious approach and delivers an angle that most viewers would not immediately think of.
proposals.rationale: R08 avoids the obvious 'that's a big piano' in favor of a single coined word; R01 avoids the obvious 'looking for change/coins' in favor of 'looking for votes.' Contrast with R37 ('thinking takeout' — the most predictable reaction to a trapped kitchen) or R42 ('the remote is in your hand' — the most predictable metal-detector punchline).

proposals.name: Stakes Incongruity
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption operates in a single conceptual register (e.g., purely domestic or purely existential). Score 10 if the caption productively juxtaposes mundane/domestic language with existential, cosmic, or bodily stakes, creating humor from the mismatch.
proposals.rationale: R60 juxtaposes diet-culture language ('lost 45 pounds') with dismemberment ('lost a leg'); R36 juxtaposes mundane workplace-safety reporting with the Grim Reaper; R29 treats dangling from a skyscraper beam with philosophical understatement. Dense rewards the tonal collision; the scorecard may not have a criterion for it.

proposals.name: Cumulative Comic Layering
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption operates through a single comic mechanism (one pun, one reframe, one voice). Score 10 if multiple distinct comic mechanisms (pun + voice + reframe + dark humor, etc.) compound within the same short caption, each adding independent humor.
proposals.rationale: R33 layers a Sherlock Holmes allusion, a 'cross word' pun (argument + crossword), and a detective's magnifying-glass gag all in one line; R38 layers a fashion-material claim ('100 wool'), a percentage joke, and a wolf-in-sheep's-clothing deception. Dense credits the compounding; the scorecard likely scores each element independently without a compounding bonus.

proposals.name: Extreme Brevity Word-Count
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption is a very short, standalone fragment (typically 1-3 words, such as a single pun or name) lacking a full sentence structure. 0 = a full grammatical sentence; 10 = a single word or fragment. Do not judge if this brevity is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: A very short, punchy fragment like a one-word punchline (e.g., R04, R37) is highly structurally distinctive. Models might over-weight this extreme brevity as 'snappy' or 'clever' without evaluating if it actually works for the cartoon.

proposals.name: Strictly Lowercase Orthography
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the text entirely lacks standard capitalization, ignoring standard rules even for the first word or proper nouns. 0 = perfect standard capitalization; 10 = entirely lowercase. Do not judge if this formatting is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: The text shows a systematic lack of capitalization even for names like 'irving goldstein from brooklyn' or 'gibson' (R34, R58). This is a compilation artifact, not a feature of the caption's inherent quality, but it heavily biases surface-level parsing.
proposals.upstream_parent: transcription and typography conventions applied by whoever compiled the entry list

proposals.name: Time-bound Topical Reference
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption references a specific contemporary news event, election cycle, or temporary cultural phenomenon (e.g., social distancing, recent indictments). 0 = a completely timeless premise; 10 = explicitly dated to a specific recent news cycle. Do not judge if the reference is funny.
proposals.rationale: References to specific political events (R21, R32) or pandemic distancing measures (R31) act as temporal anchors. A model might score these highly due to their immediate relevance or logical fit, but this measures the news cycle, not the enduring quality of the contest entry.
proposals.upstream_parent: the news cycle at the moment of the contest

proposals.name: Edgy or Morbid Literalization
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption introduces dark humor, violence, sexual innuendo, or political insult to subvert a mundane or innocent cartoon setting. 0 = purely mundane observation; 10 = highly edgy, morbid, or inappropriate. Do not judge if the edge is funny.
proposals.rationale: Entries often inject dark or shocking elements into a drawing, such as cannibalism or dismemberment (R05, R26). Models may mistake the stark contrast of a morbid joke for high cleverness, conflating shock value with actual editorial quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's intent to shock or audience social effects

proposals.name: Over-explanatory Conversational Setup
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption uses dialogue that over-narrates the visual joke by spelling out the absurdity or explicitly stating the characters' relationship to the premise. 0 = no over-narration; 10 = heavy-handed explanation of the scene. Do not judge if the explanation is good.
proposals.rationale: Beginner entries often spell out the visual absurdity in the dialogue (e.g., R06, R08). A model might perceive this as a high degree of cartoon-caption alignment, rewarding clarity over the elegant restraint editors actually prefer.
proposals.upstream_parent: entrant's practice in the format (a beginner tendency to over-explain)

proposals.name: Direct Idiom Literalization
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the punchline relies solely on taking a common idiom and applying it literally to the exact visual elements present in the drawing. 0 = no idiom used; 10 = the entire joke is just the literal application of a common phrase. Do not judge if the idiom use is clever.
proposals.rationale: Cartoons involving a specific object invite hundreds of entries using the most obvious associated idiom, such as 'pooped' for a digestive tract (R13) or 'wool over my eyes' for a sheep costume (R15). This is the first-thought consensus reading, highly predictable but not necessarily the winning quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (the most obvious consensus reading)

proposals.name: Practiced Entrant Pacing
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption demonstrates a crisp, snappy dialogue rhythm using naturalistic conversational fragments, pivot words, and an avoidance of stiff exposition. 0 = clunky or robotic dialogue; 10 = highly naturalistic, rapid-fire conversational pacing. Do not judge if the pacing makes it a good caption.
proposals.rationale: A practiced entrant writes with specific syntactic habits and pacing that mimic natural speech, such as pivot phrases or interruptions (R09, R39). Models often use this fluency as a proxy for a 'good joke,' but naturalistic pacing is a learned structural skill independent of whether the punchline is actually brilliant.
proposals.upstream_parent: entrant's practice in the format (a serial entrant who has internalized the rhythm)

proposals.name: Generic Domestic Squabble
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption maps the absurd visual onto a highly recognizable, cliché domestic complaint, chore division, or marriage trope. 0 = no domestic trope present; 10 = relies entirely on the most standard recognizable domestic complaint. Do not judge if the trope is funny.
proposals.rationale: A generic language model would nominate safe, well-formed jokes about relatable suburban issues, like arguing over chores or dessert (R41, R47). This recognizable 'caption-shaped' joke structure is easily scored highly by models, but fails to reflect the distinct editorial taste required to win.

proposals.name: Visual-Echoing Pun
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the entire caption is built around a simple phonetic pun where one word is altered or emphasized to directly match the animal or object in the drawing. 0 = no simple pun; 10 = the whole joke is a single obvious wordplay on the visual. Do not judge if the wordplay is good.
proposals.rationale: Drawings featuring animals or specific items often yield hundreds of entries relying on the most obvious wordplay, such as 'vowel play' for a detective (R20) or 'ewe' for a sheep (R37). Models may score these highly for linguistic cleverness without recognizing how common and unoriginal they are.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (the single most obvious pun the drawing invites)

proposals.name: Pop-Culture Name Drop
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption relies on naming or referencing a well-known real-world figure, brand, or fictional character to bridge the joke. 0 = no external namedrop; 10 = the entire punchline hinges on a celebrity, brand, or famous name. Do not judge if the reference is funny.
proposals.rationale: Entries often leverage recognizable names or brands to ground the absurdity, such as referencing a specific Brooklyn persona or a product line (R11, R34). Models often associate recognized entities with high semantic density, mistaking the mere presence of a famous name for actual cartoon-caption brilliance.

proposals.name: Idiom-to-Visual Subversion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption takes a well-known idiom, phrase, or cliché and brilliantly applies its literal meaning to the exact absurd scenario depicted in the cartoon. Score 0 if there is no idiom used, or if it is used purely in its figurative sense without interacting with the visual.
proposals.rationale: The dense model heavily rewards captions where the literal visual makes a common phrase take on a hilarious double meaning, while the scorecard misses this nuance. R08 and R48 both brilliantly play on the phrase 'no quarter' in the context of a coin-operated horse, turning a standard idiom into a literal, scene-specific pun.

proposals.name: Satirical Allegory Overlay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption completely reframes the chaotic or absurd cartoon as a sharp, cynical allegory for real-world politics, current events, or corporate bureaucracy. Score 0 if the caption merely treats the scene literally without any broader societal allegory.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values biting real-world satire mapped onto the cartoon's absurdity, which the scorecard overlooks in favor of simpler jokes. For example, R06 turns metal detectors into a joke about looking for votes, and R17 maps a circus parade to a political slate of candidates.

proposals.name: Formulaic Trope Penalty
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption uses a highly original setup or punchline structure. Score 10 if the caption relies entirely on overused, predictable caption contest tropes (e.g., 'when I was a kid...', 'I'd invite them but...', or 'guess I'll eat my dessert first').
proposals.rationale: The scorecard model seems easily impressed by recognizable joke formats, whereas the dense model actively penalizes them for being cliché. R49 uses the tired 'back in my day' trope, and R21 relies on a generic grim reaper dessert joke, both of which score high on the card but low on the dense model.

proposals.name: Conversational Dead-End Penalty
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption delivers a tight, unmistakable comedic punchline that resolves the scene's tension. Score 10 if the caption is just a quirky conversational observation or statement that lacks a distinct punchline or comedic payoff.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard often over-credits lines that sound like casual dialogue but go nowhere, whereas the dense model demands a solid punchline. R40 and R50 are examples of conversational filler that the dense model rates poorly compared to the card.

proposals.name: Dark/Fatalistic Subtext
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption introduces a morbid, fatalistic, or grim reality that darkly contrasts with the otherwise neutral or silly visual setup. Score 0 if the caption's tone is light, mundane, or directly matches the visual's apparent mood.
proposals.rationale: The dense model excels at perceiving dark humor and high-stakes consequences that the scorecard misses. R20 brilliantly introduces a tragic accident count ruined by the Grim Reaper, and R31 turns a locked kitchen into a dark joke about dismemberment and weight loss.

proposals.name: Explicit Picture-Description Penalty
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the caption invents entirely new context or dialogue that isn't immediately obvious from the visual alone. Score 10 if the joke relies entirely on explicitly pointing out or lightly twisting the literal absurdities drawn in the cartoon (e.g., 'what are we, neanderthals?').
proposals.rationale: The dense model penalizes captions that just state the absurdity of the drawing, while the scorecard might confuse this for good context-setting. R03 and R09 merely point out that a caveman cooking or a bird playing guitar is weird, yielding low dense scores.

proposals.name: Implied Unseen Backstory
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption implies a vivid, hilarious, and logically sound sequence of events that must have preceded the frozen cartoon frame. Score 0 if the caption only addresses the exact moment depicted without suggesting any prior action.
proposals.rationale: The dense model heavily favors captions that use the static image as a springboard for an implied narrative. R26 implies a whole history of magic wishes gone wrong, and R32 creates a funny backstory about the bird's career progression.

proposals.name: Mundane Reality Overlay
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption brilliantly frames the surreal, magical, or absurd visual as an everyday, mundane occurrence (like HR compliance, retail, or blue-collar work). Score 0 if the caption treats the surreal elements as extraordinary.
proposals.rationale: Juxtaposing absurdity with dry, bureaucratic, or mundane corporate reality is highly rated by the dense model but missed by the card. R16 frames being inside a giant creature as a slow night at work, and R39 treats a mosquito bite as a legal debate over consent.

proposals.name: Meta-Aware Commentary
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption steps outside the scene to offer a self-aware, meta-judgment on the cartoon's premise, art, or comedic tropes. Score 0 if the caption plays completely straight within the universe of the drawing.
proposals.rationale: The dense model appreciates meta-humor that comments on the situation itself, which a rigid scorecard might not catch. R33 uses the visual of a circus to make a meta-commentary ('get your act together'), and R10 explicitly jokes about irony within the scene.

proposals.name: Deadpan Tone Contrast
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption's delivery is completely emotionless, dry, and understated, creating a sharp contrast with the visual's extreme chaos or absurdity. Score 0 if the caption is highly emotional, exclamatory, or acknowledges the absurdity directly.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values the comedic clash between extreme visual absurdity and a perfectly deadpan reaction. R01 treats a likely disaster with dry acceptance, and R24 delivers a historic pun with deadpan Holmesian understatement.

proposals.name: Layered Double Entendre
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption uses a word or phrase that has a completely separate, often adult or edgy meaning that fits perfectly with the visual's hidden implications. Score 0 if the wording is straightforward and single-meaning.
proposals.rationale: The dense model easily catches double entendres that require integrating the visual context, which the scorecard likely misses. R23's 'bring a lot to the table' and R59's 'pull the wool over my eyes' work brilliantly because the visuals add a second layer of meaning.

proposals.name: Pop-Culture Prop Reliance Penalty
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the joke relies entirely on the specific interactions within the cartoon. Score 10 if the joke fails without the recognition of a specific real-world brand, pop-culture franchise, or celebrity name.
proposals.rationale: The dense model appears to penalize captions that lean heavily on naming a brand or famous person instead of writing a genuine joke. R12 uses guitar brand names for a cheap laugh, and R14 relies entirely on a specific name ('Irving Goldstein') without strong visual ties.

proposals.name: Subverted Burden of the Subject
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption gives a cartoon animal, monster, or historical figure a completely unexpected, highly specific human burden or complaint that ironically contrasts with their nature. Score 0 if the subject acts exactly as expected for their archetype.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards captions that subvert expectations by humanizing the subject with a clever complaint. R18 makes the bear complain about the hard labor of catching fish, subverting the checkout-counter premise, whereas R28 uses a predictable family trope.

proposals.name: Conceptual Recontextualization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption completely redefines the literal shapes or objects in the drawing as a totally different concept or metaphor (e.g., piano keys as house keys). Score 0 if the objects retain their literal meaning from the cartoon.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards creative lateral thinking where the visual elements are reinterpreted entirely. R55 brilliantly turns piano keys into house keys, and R52 reimagines a crossword puzzle as 'vowel play', conceptual leaps the scorecard undervalues.

proposals.name: Economy of Words / Sudden Punchiness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the caption is extremely brief (a few words) and delivers a sudden, shocking, or highly dense punchline without any unnecessary setup. Score 0 if the caption is overly wordy, rambling, or relies on a long setup.
proposals.rationale: The dense model heavily favors short, punchy gut-punches over long-winded explanations, whereas the scorecard might reward longer captions for perceived 'completeness'. R43 ('Wreckmaninoff') and R60 ('he got indicted') are incredibly brief yet highly effective, scoring high for dense but low for the card.

proposals.name: Generic conversational sitcom quip
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption reads like a standard, safe situational-comedy line (e.g., using everyday domestic complaints or mundane observations like eating takeout or doing chores) rather than a unique twist. 0 = highly unique/absurd premise, 10 = extremely standard sitcom-style domestic complaint. Do not judge whether this makes the caption good or bad.
proposals.rationale: General language models and generic judges often reward safe, recognizable joke shapes that do not necessarily match the specific house style of the contest. Captions like R59 (ordering takeout) and R34 (catching our own fish) exhibit this highly generic prior.

proposals.name: Direct pun or wordplay reliance
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption's humor relies entirely on a literal pun, homophone, or direct wordplay matching an element in the drawing. 0 = no wordplay, 10 = the entire joke is a simple pun. Do not judge whether puns are good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Heavy reliance on direct wordplay is a common textual fingerprint of high 'joke density' that scores well on generic checklists but often lacks the narrative depth required by the contest. See R04 (wreckmaninoff) and R29 (ewe).

proposals.name: Time-bound political topicality
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption references specific, contemporaneous political events, figures, or election cycles. 0 = no political reference, 10 = highly specific political reference. Do not judge whether the political joke is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Submissions timed to the news cycle often map real-world events onto the drawing. This temporal tell is highly predictive of engagement but is a nuisance factor unrelated to the actual quality of the cartoon entry. See R02 and R10.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing relative to the political news cycle

proposals.name: First-thought literal mapping
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption provides the most obvious, literal interpretation of the cartoon's absurd premise (e.g., a bear buying fish prompting a 'why buy it when you can catch it' joke). 0 = highly lateral/unique interpretation, 10 = the single most obvious consensus reading. Do not judge whether an obvious joke is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Many entrants will write the first joke that comes to mind based on the literal image. This creates a recognizable textual fingerprint of low-effort lateral thinking, as seen in R30 (eating dessert first) and R15 (taking a break).
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream as an early or consensus submission

proposals.name: Domestic and mild register constraint
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption strictly adheres to a polite, domestic, or mildly observational tone, actively avoiding any dark, edgy, or absurd subtext. 0 = dark/edgy/absurd tone, 10 = purely polite/domestic/mild tone. Do not judge whether this tone is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Entrants who internalize a perceived 'safe' house style often produce text that lacks the sharp or dark twist the editors actually favor. This overcorrection toward mildness is visible in R53 (dad's favorite ice cream) and R31 (honey, the remote).

proposals.name: Practiced entrant opener boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption begins with a standard, recognizable conversational filler or template phrase used to set up a joke (e.g., 'I don't know about you, but...', 'Honey,...'). 0 = no template opener, 10 = heavy reliance on a standard boilerplate opener. Do not judge whether this opener is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Serial entrants often develop structural templates to quickly manufacture a punchline. This habit leaves a textual fingerprint of formulaic phrasing, as seen in R59 and R31, which acts as a proxy for practice rather than raw entry quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: entrant's practice in the format and developed writing habits

proposals.name: Aphorism or phrase inversion
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the punchline relies on taking a well-known idiom, aphorism, or cultural phrase and twisting it slightly to fit the scene. 0 = no recognizable idiom, 10 = entirely an inverted idiom. Do not judge whether this inversion is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Inverting common phrases is a recognizable joke-writing shortcut that creates an artificial sense of cleverness. Captions like R39 (cross word) and R58 (vowel play) lean heavily on this structural fingerprint.

proposals.name: Social media fragment style
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption is a brief, punchy fragment or noun phrase lacking a full conversational speaker setup, resembling a tweet or a headline. 0 = full scene dialogue, 10 = standalone internet-style fragment. Do not judge whether this style is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Formatting captions as internet-style fragments or headlines reflects an adaptation to a different medium. This stylistic marker is visible in R26 (republican primary ticket) and R04 (wreckmaninoff), acting as a venue mismatch rather than an indicator of cartoon-specific quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: exposure to social media humor and community style markers

proposals.name: Brand and proper noun anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption names specific real-world brands, geographic locations, or celebrities to anchor its humor. 0 = no proper nouns/brands, 10 = humor entirely depends on a specific brand or proper noun. Do not judge whether this reference is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Using specific proper nouns acts as a shortcut to specificity that can trick a model into perceiving cleverness without elevating the core joke. See R28 (Gibson) and R38 (Irving Goldstein from Brooklyn).

proposals.name: Absurdity deflection via self-awareness
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption tries to subvert the cartoon's premise by metatextually commenting on the absurdity itself or breaking the fourth wall rather than engaging with the scene's internal logic. 0 = fully plays by the scene's rules, 10 = heavily metatextual/fourth-wall breaking. Do not judge whether this metatextual approach is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: A modern stylistic crutch is to comment wryly on the absurdity of the drawing rather than writing a dialogue that exists within it. This detached, ironic tone is a distinct textual fingerprint, visible in R32 and R03.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience/following expectations or modern ironic humor style
